result:
The morning light hit the kitchen counter at exactly the wrong angle, and I realized I'd been measuring my life in coffee rings and the particular silence of a house where no one else was awake yet. There's a geometry to loneliness that no one teaches you—the way it fills corners first, pools in the spaces between furniture, climbs the walls like a slow tide.

I used to think memory worked like a filing cabinet. Now I know it's more like a garden that refuses to be planned. The tomatoes volunteer where the roses should be. The compost of old embarrassments heats up without warning, steaming in the cold dawn. I am forty-three years old and I still wake up sometimes convinced I have a math test I haven't studied for, the anxiety so real I can smell the chalk dust, taste the metallic tang of the fountain water in that hallway with the green linoleum.

My grandmother kept a jar of buttons on her dresser. Not useful buttons, not spare ones for emergencies. These were archaeological. A mother-of-pearl disk from a coat she wore to a dance in 1957. A wooden toggle from a sweater that smelled of her husband's pipe tobacco. A bright red plastic circle from a child's coat—my mother's, I think, though the story shifted depending on the day and the light. She would run them through her fingers like worry beads, and I understand that now. The body needs something to occupy itself when the mind is busy falling through time.

I read once that the human heart can continue beating for several minutes after being removed from the chest. I don't know if this is true and I don't want to verify it. But I think about it when I'm in traffic, when the radio plays something I wasn't expecting, when the song is from a year that no longer exists except in the amber of melody. The heart doesn't know. The heart keeps going, stubborn, stupid, magnificent. It doesn't understand that the rest of the system has quit, has moved on, has become something else.

My neighbor practices saxophone on Tuesday evenings. He's not good. He may never be good. But there's something in the reaching that matters, in the sound of someone trying to bend air into meaning. I sit on my porch and listen to him wrestle with "Blue Moon" and I want to tell him that perfection is the enemy of the actual, that the cracked notes are where the light gets in, but we don't have that kind of relationship. We have the kind where we nod at the mailboxes, where we comment on the weather with the sincerity of people who have nothing else to say and find that, somehow, it is enough.

The cat sleeps in a patch of sun that moves across the floor like a clock made of warmth. I have never been as committed to anything as she is to this migration, this following of light across the hours. She does not check her phone. She does not wonder if she should be doing something else, something more productive, more aligned with her goals. She is fully in the sun, and then the sun moves, and she moves with it. There is no story she tells herself about this. There is only the warmth, and then the seeking of warmth.

I am tired of the word "journey." I am tired of the word "authentic." I want a language that hasn't been focus-grouped, that doesn't come with a hashtag attached. I want to describe the feeling of finding a photograph of yourself as a child and not recognizing the eyes, the particular hope in them that you have somehow lost without noticing, like a sweater left on a bus. What is the word for that? We don't have it. We have "nostalgia," which is too sweet, too much like candy. What I feel is more like archaeology. More like digging through layers and finding evidence of a civilization that used the same name I use but was otherwise incomprehensible.

Last week I found a grocery list in a used book. *Milk. Eggs. Call Sarah. Band-Aids. Something for the garden.* I kept it. I don't know why. Maybe because it was proof that someone else was trying to hold things together with paper and ink, that the ordinary emergencies of being alive don't require heroic language, just a list, just the next small thing. Call Sarah. What happened when Sarah was called? I'll never know. The book was a novel about a man who builds a boat in his attic, which is impossible, which is the point. The boat is never finished. The man dies with sawdust in his hair and the attic door nailed shut by his children, who don't understand, who think he was crazy.

But he wasn't crazy. He was building a boat. In the wrong place, with the wrong tools, for a sea that didn't exist. And isn't that what we're all doing, in our different attics, with our different impossible materials? The boat is not the point. The building is the point. The sawdust in the hair. The refusal to stop even when the dimensions are wrong, even when the water never comes.

The coffee is cold now. The light has moved past the counter, into the living room, where it illuminates the dust I keep meaning to address. I will not address it today. Today I will do something else, something equally small and equally important, something that will not appear in any account of my life but without which the whole structure would collapse. I will buy milk. I will call someone, though not Sarah, who is a stranger and probably doesn't want to hear from me. I will run my fingers through buttons I don't remember acquiring. I will listen to bad saxophone and think about boats in attics, about hearts that beat in empty spaces, about the stubborn, beautiful, useless persistence of trying to make something where nothing was before.

The cat has moved. The sun has moved. I will move too, eventually, when the coffee is gone, when the list is made, when the next small thing presents itself and I answer, as I always do, as I will until I can't, with yes, with now, with this.
